subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage:
Day 1. In their first week in the new flat, Ujjwal and Lavanya made pancakes badly and ate them standing up. “Every Sunday?” Lavanya said. “Every Sunday,” Ujjwal said.
Day 8. Their neighbours from downstairs smelled burnt batter and knocked. Six people squeezed around a table meant for two, and the pancakes were still lopsided.
Day 30. Lavanya's cousin phoned on Saturday night to ask, “Is the pancake thing still on tomorrow?” Ujjwal had already bought extra flour. By then two neighbours brought fruit, and a child had drawn a pancake calendar and stuck it to the fridge.

qa.q: How many people squeezed around the table on Day 8?
qa.a: Six people squeezed around the table.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal buy extra flour before Lavanya's cousin phoned?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt happy and hopeful about the Sunday pancakes growing and wanted the weekly gathering to go on, so the tradition felt like theirs.

qa.q: What choice at the start turned two people into a small community?
qa.a: Ujjwal and Lavanya agreed on a regular time, every Sunday, and let the neighbours join when they knocked.

qa.q: How might the neighbours from downstairs have felt when they knocked?
qa.a: The neighbours may have been curious and hoping to be invited, and felt welcomed when six people squeezed around the table.

grounding: A newly married couple builds their own tradition, a weekly breakfast, which turns a group of individuals into a community.

subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage: “Come, sit,” said Hafsa, senior clerk in the accounts office. “When I joined, nobody spoke over lunch; people ate at their desks. So on my second Thursday I brought a box of biscuits and put it in the middle of the table. Nobody touched it. Kavitha, the quiet clerk, was the first. She took one and made a joke about the tea. By the third Thursday, four of us shared the table. By the sixth, the manager brought his own. Thirty years later, the Thursday tea is older than half the staff. You start small, and you keep turning up, beta.”

qa.q: What did Hafsa put in the middle of the table on the second Thursday?
qa.a: Hafsa put a box of biscuits in the middle of the table.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have been feeling when Kavitha was the first to take a biscuit?
qa.a: Kavitha, the quiet clerk, was probably a little shy and brave, willing to be the first to take part and start a conversation with a joke.

qa.q: What choice by Hafsa began the tradition, and what kept it going?
qa.a: Hafsa brought biscuits and put them in the middle of the table, and then kept turning up every Thursday.

qa.q: How might the manager have seen the Thursday tea by the sixth week?
qa.a: The manager seems to have wanted to be part of it, since he brought his own contribution.

grounding: A newly employed person starts a small weekly tea tradition that turns a group of individuals into a community, told by an elder.
